articles.text: The sporting world has again come forth from its winter quarters and from time to time a column of "Sporting Notes" may be expected by our readers.
articles.summary: The paper promises occasional Sporting Notes now that spring has come.

articles.text: Wednesday the 15th of April, has been selected by Governor Pierce as Arbor day. It is especially requested that everyone should observe this day and plant as many trees as possible. For the purpose of doing more effectual work in this direction we will in our next issue call a meeting to be held in the Cow Boy office, to see what our citizens are willing to do in this direction.
articles.summary: Governor Pierce names April 15 Arbor Day; the Cow Boy will call a tree-planting meeting.

articles.text: The latest report states that Gen. Grant's condition is much improved. It is very doubtful if he can live long but the hearts of a whole nation quicken at the joyful news. At every opportunity he works on his history of the war and it is sincerly hoped that he will live long enough to complete it. His financial troubles and present sickness have buried in oblivon all the factional enmity toward him and now in his weak old age he is again gaining the place in the hearts of his countrymen that he held after the war.
articles.summary: Editorial on General Grant's illness and his work on his war history.

articles.text: The Mandan Pioneer makes us tired. It is raising a constant howl against ready-prints and then fills up three-fourths of its space with "snakes." The ready-prints contain the latest news in condensed form, besides much other interesting and live reading matter. The "snakes" are mostly old, mil-dewed stories and are at best but poor "filling," and scarcely ever make a good impression on the paper, a point which the Pioneer never wastes its valuable time in getting in any event. Cork up on ready-prints or be consistent and discard "snakes,' Mr. Pioneer.
articles.summary: Packard defends ready-print pages against the Mandan Pioneer's criticism.

articles.text: The Dominion government is reaping the result of its tyrannical policy toward settlers and now has a good-sized rebellion on its hands in the Saskatchewan country. The uprising is headed by Louis Riel, of Red River fame and is raised because of the non-settlement of land claims. Riel was sent for from Montana to direct the settlers and for a long time counseled law-abiding measures. These utterly failed in their object and rebellion is the result. The rebels are well-armed and will make a desperate struggle for their rights. The Dominion troops and artillery are being sent forward and probably by this time an encounter has taken place.
articles.summary: Editorial on Louis Riel's rebellion in the Saskatchewan country.

articles.text: A great deal of newspaper talk has been wasted over the prospective removal of Governor Pierce and as to who his successor will probably be. If the prospect worried the newspapers as little as it does the governor much less space would be occupied in its consideration and much less reason could be given by the president for his removal if all the governor's would-be friends would stop showing the likelihood of his removal and trying the hit-or-miss style of hewing out gubernatorial timber for the purpose of standing in with a new administration. President Cleveland has been nearly consistent in his practice of civil service reform rules, which he interprets about as follows: Office-holders should be removed for inefficiency, for mal-feasance of office or for taking an active part in politics, or for having retained office on account of the votes he controlled. Not a solitary one of these reasons can be brought to the governor's door and the president will have to find new reasons for the appointment of a Democrat as governor of Dakota. We believe the president is in earnest about civil service reform and consequently that Gilbert A Pierce will be governor for the next three years.
articles.summary: Packard predicts Governor Gilbert A. Pierce will keep office under Cleveland's civil service policy.

articles.text:
"In the wild, unfettered west, beware of the man who never carries arms, never gets drunk, and always minds his own business. He don't go around shooting out the gas, or intimidating a kindergarten school; but when a brave frontiersman, with a revolver in each hand and a bowie down the back of his neck, insults a modest young lady, and needs to be thrown through a plate-glass window and then walked over by the populace, call in the silent man, who dares to wear a clean shirt and human clothes."—[Bill Nye.

With all his humor and fiction, the above article shows that Bill Nye occasionally uses a good deal of sound common sense in his articles. It can be put down as a fact that four-fifths of the reckless shooting done in the west, is the work of some sap-headed tender-foot who wants to pose as a bad man. As long as these characters tackle other pilgrims, their true charactsr is not exposed and the police papers of the east will come out with another account of the way a bad man held up a guileless tender-foot, and the goal of another would-be bad man's happiness is reached by this publication. At some time, each one of these Police Gazette bad men will meet the quiet, unarmed man spoken of in the above article and each one will get his head everlastingly swelled externally to balance the internal swelling. This is the most accommodating country in the world to the man who is looking for a fight and the only reason these men are not exposed sooner is that they are careful to pick upon men whom they know will not resist.
articles.summary: Bill Nye quotation on the quiet western man, with Packard's comment that most reckless shooting is done by tenderfeet posing as bad men.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES. Strayed or Stolen.
articles.text: From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: Notice of John Pohl's bay horse strayed or stolen from Little Missouri in July 1884; $25 reward.

articles.summary: Musselshell and Yellowstone cattlemen to hold round-up meeting at Billings April 5.

articles.summary: S. A. Marney of the Stockgrowers' Journal passed through Medora.

articles.summary: Car-load cattle rates from St. Paul to Medora are $75 this season.

articles.text: Mr. Stotts, of Spearfish, started home Monday morning. He has been in Iowa buying cattle, all thoroughbreds or high grades, for his Redwater ranch in the Hills.
articles.summary: Mr. Stotts of Spearfish left for home after buying blooded cattle in Iowa.

articles.text: The Stockgrowers' Journal reports that 100,000 head of Texas cattle will be ready for a northern movement within the next sixty days. It is doubtful, however, if a solitary head will be forwarded, as the quarantine laws of Colorado, Kansas and New Mexico are prohibitary.
articles.summary: 100,000 Texas cattle ready to move north, but quarantine laws likely block them.

articles.text: It seems strange that some of our stockmen do not drive in a good herd of cow-horses and keep them for sale. There is right now a large demand for them and over two hundred could have been sold on the river since last fall. Our stockmen are waking up to the fact that there is no economy in buying cheap cow-horses and there is now a ready sale for first-class animals.
articles.summary: Strong demand for cow-horses on the Little Missouri.

articles.text: We are in receipt of a letter from Julius LeMoyne, expressing regret that he could not attend the meeting of stockmen here on April 1. He is in favor of seven or eight good bulls rather than ten to the hundred of she cattle. He is also very favorably impressed with the merits of polled cattle for the range. He intends being in Medora some time in May.
articles.summary: Julius LeMoyne writes he cannot attend the April 1 stockmen's meeting but plans to visit Medora in May.

articles.text: Action should be taken at the coming meeting of the Little Missouri association toward getting a territorial veterinary surgeon. It will be two years before the legislature meets again but something can be done now toward the making of such an office. Such action is necessary because in all probobility a territorial veterinary surgeon will be appointed at the next session of the legislature and it is important that a competent man be appointed and not some ignoramus whose chief qualification is his political record.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy urges the stockmen's association to push for a competent territorial veterinary surgeon.

articles.text:
We are in receipt of a letter from Theodore Roosevelt and the printed by-laws of the Little Missouri river Stockmen's Association. In the by-laws we notice that the number of bulls to the hundred cows has been changed from ten to seven. The letter contains the following official call:

"A meeting of the Little Missouri Stockmen's Association is hereby called for 11 A. M., Wednesday, April 1, 1885, to be held in Pennell Hall, Medora, Dak. Matters connected with the spring round-up will come up for discussion.".

THEODORE ROOSEVELT.
Chairman.
articles.summary: Theodore Roosevelt, as chairman, sends the printed by-laws and calls a Little Missouri Stockmen's Association meeting for April 1, 1885, at Pennell Hall.

articles.text: By the sale of Billy Paddock's ranch to [B. S.?] Lamb and with the stocking of this range the Little Missouri river front will be pretty well occupied for fifty miles up the river and fifty miles down. To our mind, however, there are other ranges off the river, tributary to Medora that are as good as, if not superior to anything on the river. One can scarcely go amiss in locating a range six or eight miles back from the river provided water can be obtained in good quantity. From the nature of the country, there is little danger of enough cattlemen coming in on the river to overstock the ranges.
articles.summary: Billy Paddock's ranch is sold to Lamb; the river front is nearly fully occupied, but good back ranges remain.

articles.text: The Montana legislature at the recent session passed a bill relating to stock inspection that, from all we can see, will be a great advantage. The territory is divided into two districts; Custer, Yellowstone and Dawson counties forming the first, and Choteau, Meagher and Lewis and Clark counties, forming the second. For each of these counties a cattle commissioner is appointed by the governor, each commissioner to be an owner of cattle, and all to form a territorial board of stock commissioners who shall have general control of stock interests and be authorized to punish any unlawful act against such interests. The board is authorized to appoint as many detectives as it sees proper who are empowered to make arrests as they may be necessary. One and one-half mills on the valuation of all stock is taxed against owners to pay expenses as incurred by these detectives. The commissioners are to receive no salary but the detectives will be salaried.
articles.summary: Summary of Montana's new stock inspection law and board of stock commissioners.

articles.text:
We presume the by-laws of our association are pretty generally known as they were published at the time of the December meeting. For the benefit of those who were not there we republish them:

1.—This Association shall be known as The Little Missouri river Stockmen's Association.

2.—The object of this Association is to advance the interests of stockgrowers and dealers in live stock of all kinds in western Dakota, and for the purpose of the protection of the same against frauds and swindlers, and to prevent the stealing, taking, and driving away of horned cattle, sheep, horses, and other stock from the rightful owners thereof, and to enforce the stock laws of the Territory of Dakota.

3.—The officers of the Association shall consist of a Chairman and Vice-Chairman, elected annually at the first meeting held after the fall round-up, and a Secretary, elected at each meeting, whose work is to be superintended by the Chairman.

4.—The representation in the Association is to be by firms, each firm being entitled to but one vote.

5.—There shall be at least two meetings of the Association annually; to be held at the time and place appointed by the Association; and at the request in writing of any three members of the Association a special meeting shall be called by the Chairman, who shall, however, give at least one week's notice thereof. Seven members shall constitute a quorum for transaction of business.

ORDER OF BUSINESS.

I. Calling the roll.
II. Reading minutes of last meeting.
III. Election of new members.
IV. Unfinished business.
V. Reports of officers and committees.
VI. Election of officers.
VII. General business.

7.—No member shall gather cattle on any range not his own during the months between December 1st and the date of general spring round-up, without giving due notice a reasonable time beforehand to the other ranchmen of the neighborhood.

8.—In order to attain greater efficiency in round-ups, we hereby agree to place our men under the orders of the foreman of the round-up, so long as they remain with it, and in case of refusal by any man to do faithfully and well the duty assigned to him, or to obey the orders given to him by the foreman, in driving, cutting out, and other work, we hereby authorize the foreman of any round-up to prohibit any man so offending from any further participation in said work.

9.—It is the sense of this Association, and is hereby made binding on its members, that any man who shall hereafter turn out any female neat cattle upon the range shall place with them, at the time of turning loose, not less than seven (7) serviceable bulls for every one hundred (100) head of female cattle which are two years old and upward at that time; and that on or before July 1st, of each year thereafter, every member shall supply the same proportion of bulls of the same usefulness and quality to all female cattle of the above age of which he may then be the owner. Proved violation of the above rule shall be deemed a proper subject for complaint, the penalty to be decided by a majority of the Association present at the next meeting.

10.—If any of the cattle companies or stockmen along the river refuse to obey the rules and by-laws of this Association, it will refuse to act with or allow them to take part in the round-up; and the captain of the round-up shall see that no stockmen debarred by action of this Association from participating in the round-up is allowed to take part in it, and he shall further see that no third party, acting in the interest of said stockman, is permitted to take part in or derive benefit from the round-up.

articles.text: We have repeatedly stated that the estimate of the cattle loss was all guess work and we are now more than ever convinced of it. We will now make the broad statement that there is not a stockman on the river who can be certain within one or two per cent., of what his loss actually is. It is utterly impossible to tell, even after the round-up. More than ever are we certain however that the loss in the Bad Lands is less than three per cent.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy says winter cattle losses in the Bad Lands are under three percent.

articles.headline: NOTICE.
articles.text:
Notice has been sent to all outside subscribers who are delinquent and if their subscription is not received by the next issue, their names will be taken from the list. It makes no difference who they are. One man's money is no better than another's and cash in advance is the only way to get the Cow Boy.

Local subscribers have not yet been notified, but the same rule applies to them.
articles.summary: Delinquent subscribers will be dropped; cash in advance only.

articles.summary: Reminder of the April 1 stockmen's meeting.

articles.summary: Peter Book back from Mandan.

articles.text: About the time Billy Jones breaks his neck running his horse across the railroad bridge he will quit it. Pat O'Hara says: "Its gettin to be a notorious job minden the holes where his cayuse's fut wint tru."

articles.text: Levi Deffebach returnd from his trip to Germany, Saturday evening. He is now stopping with his brother Rassie. His trip was not a success, neither is it as yet, a failure. A good lawyer has taken the matter in charge and is confident that he can yet get the fortune.

articles.text: We are much pleased to state that Mr. Foster will be retained here as superintendent of the slaughter-house. No better selection could possibly have been made and it is beyond question that he thoroughly understands his business and will make a success.

articles.text: Next Wednesday evening, April 1, there will be a Stockmen's ball at the Pyramid Park hotel. There is no doubt that it will be a complete success as J. B. articles.text: The cattlemen up and down the river are much encouraged over the prospect and are all coming to the conclusion that the loss is even less than the most sanguine had hoped. There is now very little danger of the weather being poor enough to cause any serious loss. With the exception of a flurry or two of snew, there will doubtless be good weather until the spring rains.
articles.summary: Cattlemen encouraged; winter losses lighter than hoped.

articles.text: John Warn, Jr., is dead. We doubt if the death of any animate being here, outside of a human, could have called forth the expressions of sorrow that were uttered at the death of this faithful dog. He was as loving and gentle as possible to canine nature. He was a friend to everyone and everyone was a friend to him. No cause can be assigned for his death except poisoning and if there lives a wretch here low-lived enough to have committed this crime; we hope he will be discovered and summarily dealt with.
articles.summary: John Warn's dog, "John Warn, Jr.," died, apparently poisoned.

articles.text: The shoot was postponed last Saturday, owing to non-attendance of a quorum of the members. Weather permitting, the contest will begin promptly at 1:30, Saturday afternoon. This will be the fourth contest in the series, taking the place of the omitted one. The final contest will take place a week from Saturday. Persons who have missed a contest will be given an opportunity to shoot off their back scores.
articles.summary: Shooting contest postponed; fourth contest set for Saturday.

articles.headline: Communication.
articles.text:
Up the River.

Editor Cow Boy

Items are scarce as goose dollars up this way. Everybody is lying on their oars, waiting for the bull round-up, though some ranch work is being done.

Deacon Wade has finished a 200 acre pasture. Ferris and Merrifield are building a corral to hold the day-herd.

Sylvane Ferris has returned from a visit to New Brunswick a little used up by dissipation we suppose, but will be around all right soon.

Will Eaton has not got done telling about the good time he had in Pittsburg and by his improved appearance, it is evident he had. Pittsburg is not noted for its temperance proclivities.

Tarbell and Bond are at their Deep Creek ranch and pushing the world ahead of them. The improvements on this ranch are very fine. Bond, the irrepressible, has renounced all evil associations and is leading a virtuous life. Nitch, Billy Jones and others would do well to follow his example.

There was a musical and dramatical entertainment at Will Dantz's ranch the other evening. Jimmy Stevenson was the Prima Donna. It is astonishing, the amount of musical talent there is lying around in the Bad Lands. The frying-pan symphony by Alden Eaton was especially fine.

Rheumatism has brought a kink in Pete Pilausie's back, which is painful to see. It is to be hoped the warm weather will soon draw it out.

Cattle are daily improving and the prospects are of a good calf crop. A few have come already, some in the late cold weather which are curiousities in their way; minus tail, ears etc.

Big horn.
articles.summary: "Big horn" reports from up the river: Wade's pasture, Ferris & Merrifield's corral, Sylvane Ferris back from New Brunswick, ranch entertainment and early calves.

articles.text:
Mouth of Cherry creek.
Little Missouri Dak., March 17, 1885.

Editor of Bad Lands Cow Boy:

A man by the name of Thomas Gibson was killed by a bear on the 16th. inst, at a point in the Bad Lands about ten miles above Cherry creek. The circumstances as near as ascertained are as follows: He in company with one William Dixon, started from Medora to come down the Little Missouri on a raft. They met with an accident, losing one rifle and all of their camp outfit and provisions. They then came to my place where they remained two days. Making another raft they went on. The next night, Dixon came back and reported his partner killed by a bear, stating that they had discovered a den while looking for deer in a clump of cedar, that Gibson, rifle in hand, had crept up to the den and when in the act of looking in had been seized and killed without having fired a shot, that having no weapon of any kind himself, he stood helplessly by and waited until the animal, finishing Gibson turned on him when he fled. The following morning we returned with Dixon and found Gibson's remains about 30 feet from the mouth of the den. From all appearances he was instantly killed. The rifle was found within six feet of the den loaded and the hammer up. No papers could be found upon the person of the dead man to indicate the whereabouts of his friends or relatives but from conversation held with him while at my place I believe him to have come to Dakota from either Wisconsin or Michegan. Dixon took charge of his effects, which consist of nothing as far as we know, but some old clothing and a val'se. We buried him on the top of a high bluff in the Bad Lands near where we found him. Further particulars, should they be wanted by his friends or relatives, can be obtained by addressing William Keldch or Chas. Tracy, Cherry creek, Little Missouri.

Yours
H. F. Pullen.
articles.summary: H. F. Pullen reports Thomas Gibson killed by a bear near Cherry Creek on March 16 while rafting down the Little Missouri with William Dixon.

articles.text: Freighters Attention! — the King jeweler, Spearfish or Deadwood, watch repairs
articles.summary: Reading notice for a Spearfish/Deadwood jeweler.

articles.headline: NOTICE.
articles.text:
Notice is hereby given that any contracts or bills made by any of the employes of the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co., will not be paid or recognized unless approved by W. F. Van Driesche, Treasurer.

Marquis de Mores, Pres't.
articles.summary: Medora Stage and Forwarding Co. will honor employee bills only if approved by Treasurer W. F. Van Driesche; signed by the Marquis de Mores.

articles.text: Cash or no Cow Boy.
articles.summary: Subscription reminder.

articles.text: The robins will soon be here.
articles.summary: Spring note.

articles.text: "Big-horn" makes a good correspondent and we hope to hear from him again.
articles.summary: Praise for correspondent "Big-horn".

articles.text: John Warn writes from Bozeman that he hopes to settle the estate there and return soon.
articles.summary: John Warn writes from Bozeman about settling an estate.

articles.text: The Marquis intends staying till after the stock meeting and will also attend the meeting at Miles City.
articles.summary: The Marquis will stay for the stock meeting and attend the Miles City meeting.

articles.text: The hotel is rapidly progressing but will hardly be completed under a month. It will be first class in every particular. Arch Boyd has leased it and will run it to the best of his ability, which as already demonstrated, is of a high order.
articles.summary: New hotel nearly a month from completion; leased by Arch Boyd.

articles.text: Ed. Drury, of Mandan, deputy-sheriff of Morton Co., came Saturday night and left for home this morning. When he came he had a Derby hat but the atmosphere seemed to be too rare to have it last. At any rate Jim O'Hannigan don't know how it lost its symmetry.
articles.summary: Morton County deputy sheriff Ed. Drury visited Medora.

articles.text: The roof of the slaughterhouse has been raised five feet to admit of easy access to the ice boxes and now Mr. Foster says it is the most complete establishment for its size in the country. Everything is on the most approved and thoroughly tested plan and is complete in every respect.
articles.summary: Slaughterhouse roof raised five feet for ice-box access.

articles.text:
General Store of the N. P. R. C. Co., Medora, Dakota — groceries, dry goods, ready-made clothing, hats, caps, canned goods, harness, saddles, tobacco and cigars, felt shoes, overshoes, boots and shoes, flour and feed, hunters' outfits a specialty
Brand: Medora Stage & F. Co. — brand on left shoulder; horses strung on stage stations between Medora and Deadwood; $25 reward for arrest and conviction of anyone dealing unlawfully with these horses
Brand: Chimney Butte Ranch, Theodore Roosevelt, Proprietor; Ferris & Merrifield, Managers — P. O. Medora; range six miles south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri (Maltese cross brand)
City Drug Store, H. M. Jorgens, Proprietor, Medora, Dak. — drugs, patent medicines, perfumery, toilet articles, notions, periodicals, stationery
Charles Cook, Medora, Dakota — fruit, candy, nuts, cigars, tobacco, pipes, cider, newspapers, periodicals, magazines, books
E. J. Owenhouse, Bozeman, Mont. — stock saddles, Concord harness, bits, spurs, chaparejos, reatas, quirts, hackamores
J. D. Garver's, Medora, Dakota — hardware and tinware
Brand: E. W. Casey, Frank S. Moore, Manager, P. O. Medora — range O'Donnell creek
Brand: Sloping Bottom Ranch, Lloyd Roberts, Proprietor, P. O. Medora
Brand: Badger Cattle Company, Howard Eaton, Manager, P. O. Medora
Brand: Dorr Clark [entry partly illegible; Spearfish, Dakota?]
Brand: Clark & Plum, Spearfish, Dakota
Brand: Little Missouri Horse Co., H. R. Tarbell, Manager, Medora
Brand: W. N. Thompson & Co., Wm. Dantz, Manager, P. O. Medora
Brand: Le Moyne Cattle Co., D. K. Wade, Manager, Medora
Brand: Soho Cattle Co., P. O. Medora
Brand: N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., Medora
Brand: Spring Creek Ranch, L. D. & B. Rumsey, J. L. Truscott, Manager
Brand: Berry, Boice & Co., Keith, Montana
Brand: E. G. Paddock, P. O. Medora
Brand: Pennell & Roberts, P. O. Medora
Brand: Lydia S. Fuller, Frank S. Moore, Manager, P. O. Medora
Brand: Custer Trail Cattle Co., F. Alden Eaton, Supt., P. O. Medora
Brand: Towers & Gudgell, P. O. Keith, Montana
Brand: Bad Lands Cattle Co., M. Wadsworth, P. O. Medora
Brand: Neimmela Ranch, Gregor Lang, Manager, P. O. Medora
articles.summary: Store ads and cattle-brand directory on page 4, including Theodore Roosevelt's Chimney Butte Ranch (Ferris & Merrifield, managers).

events.date_basis: date printed: Wednesday 15 April 1885
events.title: Arbor Day set for April 15; Cow Boy to call tree-planting meeting
events.summary: Governor Pierce selected Wednesday, April 15, as Arbor Day, and the Cow Boy said it would call a meeting at its office to organize tree planting in Medora.
events.excerpt: Wednesday the 15th of April, has been selected by Governor Pierce as Arbor day.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Cow Boy spars with the Mandan Pioneer over ready-prints
events.summary: The Cow Boy answered the Mandan Pioneer's complaints about ready-print pages, saying the Pioneer filled its own space with stale "snakes."
events.excerpt: Cork up on ready-prints or be consistent and discard "snakes,' Mr. Pioneer.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Cow Boy predicts Governor Pierce will stay in office
events.summary: Amid talk of Governor Pierce's removal by the new Cleveland administration, the Cow Boy said none of Cleveland's grounds for removal applied and predicted Pierce would serve three more years.
events.excerpt: We believe the president is in earnest about civil service reform and consequently that Gilbert A Pierce will be governor for the next three years.

events.date_basis: date printed: July 6, 1884
events.title: John Pohl's bay horse strayed or stolen from Little Missouri
events.summary: A notice offered a $25 reward for information on John Pohl's eight-year-old bay horse, branded with an anchor and a hat, which went missing from Little Missouri on July 6, 1884.
events.excerpt: A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery.

events.date_basis: date printed: March 31
events.title: Stockmen's meeting called at Glendive
events.summary: A meeting of stockmen was announced for the Merrill house in Glendive on March 31.
events.excerpt: There will be a meeting of stockmen at the Merrill house, in Glendive, March 31.

events.date_basis: date printed: April 5th
events.title: Musselshell and Yellowstone round-up meeting at Billings
events.summary: The Musselshell and Yellowstone cattlemen were to hold a round-up meeting at Billings on April 5.
events.excerpt: The Musselshell and Yellowstone cattlemen hold a round-up meeting April 5th at Billings.

events.date_basis: "last week" before Thu 26 Mar 1885
events.title: S. A. Marney of the Stockgrowers' Journal passes through Medora
events.summary: S. A. Marney of the Stockgrowers' Journal passed through Medora on his way to Miles City.
events.excerpt: S. A. Marney, of the Stockgrowers' Journal passed through Medora last week on his way to Miles City.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Mingusville cowboys out on bail
events.summary: The Mingusville cowboys who made conductor Clark "trip the light, fantastic" were out on $500 bail each.
events.excerpt: are out on bail of $500 each.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Cattle freight rates from St. Paul to Medora set at $75 a car
events.summary: Rates for shipping cattle in car-load lots from St. Paul to Medora were $75 for the season, with $5 off on ten or more cars.
events.excerpt: Cattle rates in car load lots to Medora from St. Paul, are $75 for this season

events.date_basis: "Monday" before Thu 26 Mar 1885
events.title: Mr. Stotts of Spearfish heads home after buying Iowa cattle
events.summary: Mr. Stotts of Spearfish started home Monday morning after buying thoroughbred and high-grade cattle in Iowa for his Redwater ranch in the Black Hills.
events.excerpt: He has been in Iowa buying cattle, all thoroughbreds or high grades, for his Redwater ranch in the Hills.

events.date_basis: "some time in May" after Thu 26 Mar 1885
events.title: Julius LeMoyne plans May visit to Medora
events.summary: Julius LeMoyne wrote that he could not attend the April 1 stockmen's meeting, favored seven or eight bulls to the hundred cows, and intended to be in Medora some time in May.
events.excerpt: He intends being in Medora some time in May.

events.date_basis: date printed in the call: Wednesday, April 1, 1885
events.title: Theodore Roosevelt calls Stockmen's Association meeting for April 1
events.summary: Theodore Roosevelt, chairman of the Little Missouri Stockmen's Association, sent the Cow Boy a call for a meeting at 11 a.m., Wednesday, April 1, 1885, in Pennell Hall, Medora, to discuss the spring round-up.
events.excerpt: A meeting of the Little Missouri Stockmen's Association is hereby called for 11 A. M., Wednesday, April 1, 1885, to be held in Pennell Hall, Medora, Dak.

events.date_basis: letter received before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue; no date given
events.title: Roosevelt sends printed by-laws; bull ratio cut from ten to seven
events.summary: The Cow Boy received a letter from Theodore Roosevelt with the printed by-laws of the Little Missouri River Stockmen's Association, which changed the required number of bulls per hundred cows from ten to seven.
events.excerpt: In the by-laws we notice that the number of bulls to the hundred cows has been changed from ten to seven.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Billy Paddock sells his ranch to Lamb
events.summary: Billy Paddock's ranch was sold to a man named Lamb, leaving the Little Missouri river front well occupied for fifty miles up and down the river from Medora.
events.excerpt: By the sale of Billy Paddock's ranch to [B. S.?] Lamb and with the stocking of this range the Little Missouri river front will be pretty well occupied

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Cow Boy praises Montana's new stock-inspection law
events.summary: The Cow Boy described Montana's new law creating a territorial board of stock commissioners with salaried detectives, paid for by a levy on stock, and called it a great advantage.
events.excerpt: The board is authorized to appoint as many detectives as it sees proper who are empowered to make arrests

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Stockmen's Association by-laws and member list republished
events.summary: The Cow Boy reprinted the by-laws of the Little Missouri River Stockmen's Association and its twenty members, among them the Maltese Cross brand (Ferris & Merrifield), the Elkhorn brand (Seawall & Dow) and the Marquis de Mores's N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. New members could join by handing their names to the chairman before the April meeting.
events.excerpt: Maltese Cross Brand, Ferris & Merrifield, Managers, Medora, Dakota. Elkhorn Brand, Seawall & Dow, Managers, Medora, Dakota.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Cow Boy puts Bad Lands winter cattle loss under three percent
events.summary: The Cow Boy said estimates of winter cattle losses were guesswork but was certain the loss in the Bad Lands was under three percent.
events.excerpt: More than ever are we certain however that the loss in the Bad Lands is less than three per cent.

events.date_basis: "Monday" before Thu 26 Mar 1885
events.title: Peter Book returns from Mandan
events.summary: Peter Book returned Monday from a trip to Mandan.
events.excerpt: Peter Book returned Monday from a trip to Mandan.

events.date_basis: "last night" before Thu 26 Mar 1885
events.title: Fisher's wood-pile raided
events.summary: Someone scattered Fisher's wood-pile during the night, and the paper said two or three loaded sticks would be added to the pile.
events.excerpt: Two or three loaded sticks will adorn the pile in future.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: M. Wadsworth goes west to buy cow horses
events.summary: M. Wadsworth went west to buy a band of cow horses and planned to return for the stockmen's meeting.
events.excerpt: M. Wadsworth has gone west to buy a band of cow horses.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: New tanks installed at the Medora slaughter-house
events.summary: Both new tanks were put in place and the old one moved into the new slaughter-house.
events.excerpt: Both the new tanks have been put in position and the old one is now in the new slaughter-house

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Peter Book wins building contracts including cellar at the Marquis's house
events.summary: Peter Book secured contracts for the hotel addition, the slaughter-house smoke-stack and a cellar to hold heating apparatus in the Marquis de Mores's house.
events.excerpt: a cellar in the Marquis' house to contain heating apparatus.

events.date_basis: "last Saturday" before Thu 26 Mar 1885
events.title: Johnny Chute wins potato race at the rink
events.summary: Johnny Chute won the prize in a potato race at the skating rink Saturday evening.
events.excerpt: The prize in the potato race at the rink, last Saturday evening, was won by Johnny Chute.

events.date_basis: "next Sunday" after Thu 26 Mar 1885
events.title: Rev. Schaffner of Dickinson to preach at the roller rink
events.summary: The Rev. Schaffner of Dickinson was to preach at the Medora roller rink at 7:30 Sunday evening.
events.excerpt: The Rev. Schaffner, of Dickinson, will preach at the roller rink, next Sunday evening at half-past seven.

events.date_basis: "Saturday evening" before Thu 26 Mar 1885
events.title: Levi Deffebach returns from Germany
events.summary: Levi Deffebach returned Saturday evening from a trip to Germany about a fortune; a lawyer had taken up the matter.
events.excerpt: His trip was not a success, neither is it as yet, a failure.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Mr. Foster retained as slaughter-house superintendent
events.summary: Mr. Foster was retained as superintendent of the Medora slaughter-house.
events.excerpt: Mr. Foster will be retained here as superintendent of the slaughter-house.

events.date_basis: "in about a week" after Thu 26 Mar 1885
events.title: W. B. Pryor to open boot and shoe store
events.summary: W. B. Pryor of Dickinson planned to arrive in about a week to open a boot and shoe store, and had bought a lot near the church for a shop.
events.excerpt: He has bought a lot near the church and will build a shop.

events.date_basis: date printed: April 15
events.title: Carnival and masquerade planned at roller rink
events.summary: A grand carnival and masquerade was announced for the roller rink on the evening of April 15, with a prize for the best costume.
events.excerpt: A grand carnival and masquerade will be held in the roller rink, the evening of April 15.

events.date_basis: date printed: Wednesday April 1
events.title: Stockmen's ball at the Pyramid Park hotel
events.summary: A Stockmen's ball was announced for Wednesday evening, April 1, at the Pyramid Park hotel, hosted by J. B. Walker.
events.excerpt: Next Wednesday evening, April 1, there will be a Stockmen's ball at the Pyramid Park hotel.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Cattlemen encouraged as winter loss proves light
events.summary: Cattlemen along the river concluded the winter loss was less than the most hopeful had expected, with little danger of serious loss from weather.
events.excerpt: the loss is even less than the most sanguine had hoped.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Town dog "John Warn, Jr." dies, apparently poisoned
events.summary: The dog known as John Warn, Jr., a town favorite, died, and the paper blamed poisoning.
events.excerpt: No cause can be assigned for his death except poisoning

events.date_basis: postponed "last Saturday" (21 Mar); rescheduled for "Saturday" after Thu 26 Mar 1885
events.title: Shooting contest rescheduled
events.summary: Last Saturday's shoot was postponed for want of a quorum; the fourth contest of the series was set for 1:30 Saturday afternoon, with the final a week later.
events.excerpt: Weather permitting, the contest will begin promptly at 1:30, Saturday afternoon.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Deacon Wade finishes pasture; Ferris and Merrifield build day-herd corral
events.summary: Up-river correspondent "Big horn" reported Deacon Wade had finished a 200-acre pasture and Ferris and Merrifield were building a corral to hold the day-herd, while ranchmen waited for the bull round-up.
events.excerpt: Deacon Wade has finished a 200 acre pasture. Ferris and Merrifield are building a corral to hold the day-herd.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Sylvane Ferris returns from New Brunswick
events.summary: Sylvane Ferris returned from a visit to New Brunswick, "a little used up by dissipation," the correspondent joked.
events.excerpt: Sylvane Ferris has returned from a visit to New Brunswick

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Will Eaton back from Pittsburg
events.summary: Will Eaton returned from Pittsburg and was still telling of his good time there.
events.excerpt: Will Eaton has not got done telling about the good time he had in Pittsburg

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Tarbell and Bond improving Deep Creek ranch
events.summary: Tarbell and Bond were at their Deep Creek ranch, where the improvements were described as very fine.
events.excerpt: Tarbell and Bond are at their Deep Creek ranch and pushing the world ahead of them.

events.date_basis: "the other evening"; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885
events.title: Musical entertainment at Will Dantz's ranch
events.summary: A musical and dramatic entertainment was held at Will Dantz's ranch, with Jimmy Stevenson as prima donna and a frying-pan symphony by Alden Eaton.
events.excerpt: The frying-pan symphony by Alden Eaton was especially fine.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Early calves arrive up the river
events.summary: Cattle were improving daily with prospects of a good calf crop; some early calves born in the late cold were missing tails and ears.
events.excerpt: A few have come already, some in the late cold weather which are curiousities in their way; minus tail, ears etc.

events.date_basis: "the 16th inst." in letter dated March 17, 1885
events.title: Thomas Gibson killed by a bear near Cherry Creek
events.summary: H. F. Pullen wrote that Thomas Gibson, rafting down the Little Missouri from Medora with William Dixon, was killed by a bear at a den about ten miles above Cherry Creek; Gibson was buried on a bluff near the spot.
events.excerpt: A man by the name of Thomas Gibson was killed by a bear on the 16th. inst, at a point in the Bad Lands about ten miles above Cherry creek.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Marquis de Mores's stage company restricts employee bills
events.summary: A notice signed by the Marquis de Mores as president said the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co. would not pay employee contracts or bills unless approved by Treasurer W. F. Van Driesche.
events.excerpt: will not be paid or recognized unless approved by W. F. Van Driesche, Treasurer.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: John Warn writes from Bozeman
events.summary: John Warn wrote from Bozeman that he hoped to settle the estate there and return soon.
events.excerpt: John Warn writes from Bozeman that he hopes to settle the estate there and return soon.

events.date_basis: "the stock meeting" = April 1, 1885 meeting called in this issue
events.title: Marquis de Mores to attend stock meetings at Medora and Miles City
events.summary: The Marquis de Mores intended to stay in Medora until after the stockmen's meeting and also to attend the meeting at Miles City.
events.excerpt: The Marquis intends staying till after the stock meeting and will also attend the meeting at Miles City.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Hotel construction progresses; Arch Boyd takes the lease
events.summary: The hotel under construction was progressing but would hardly be done within a month; Arch Boyd had leased it.
events.excerpt: Arch Boyd has leased it and will run it to the best of his ability

events.date_basis: "Saturday night" arrival and "this morning" departure relative to Thu 26 Mar 1885
events.title: Morton County deputy sheriff Ed. Drury visits Medora
events.summary: Ed. Drury of Mandan, deputy sheriff of Morton County, arrived Saturday night and left for home Thursday morning; his Derby hat did not survive the visit.
events.excerpt: When he came he had a Derby hat but the atmosphere seemed to be too rare to have it last.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 26 Mar 1885 issue
events.title: Slaughterhouse roof raised five feet
events.summary: The roof of the Medora slaughterhouse was raised five feet for access to the ice boxes; Mr. Foster called it the most complete establishment of its size in the country.
events.excerpt: The roof of the slaughterhouse has been raised five feet to admit of easy access to the ice boxes
